strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear empirical demonstration of error recovery gap between model scales (Figure 1)
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across three model scales (1.7B, 4B, 8B) with consistent improvements and strong baselines (GRPO, DAPO, Dr.GRPO)
Thorough ablation studies effectively isolating the contribution of fission mechanism (+1.25%) from error simulator quality (+3.62%)
High-quality data construction with hierarchical filtering, consensus verification, and detailed case studies supporting reproducibility
Sound technical approach: three-stage pipeline is well-motivated and the Error Simulator design avoids target leakage through non-revealing error descriptions
Clear presentation of algorithm with pseudocode and prompting templates; qualitative analysis shows interpretable progression from collapse to active diagnosis
Sensitivity analysis on correction trigger frequency demonstrates practical understanding of computational trade-offs
weaknesses: Severely limited evaluation scope: single benchmark (BFCL v4 Multi-Turn) with no evaluation on other tool-use benchmarks or domains despite generalization claims; unclear if results transfer to other error distributions or real-world APIs

Computational overhead inadequately addressed: no timing comparisons, FLOPs analysis, or wall-clock measurements; claims that overhead is 'partially mitigated' through trigger frequency N lack supporting cost-benefit quantification

Error Simulator quality and generalization insufficiently analyzed: no evaluation of simulator accuracy, analysis of generalization to novel error types during training, or assessment of failure modes; simulator is Qwen3-32B (large model dependency)

On-policy approximation claims are loose: errors are collected in Stage 1 and resampled in Stage 3 creating lag; LIFO helps but formal distribution shift analysis (KL divergence, importance weighting) is absent
Reward design appears ad-hoc: time-dependent weight schedules (wfmt: 2→1, wcorr: 2→3, Rlen piecewise Gaussian) lack justification or ablation studies; no sensitivity analysis to weight choices

Statistical rigor lacking: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests reported; with stochastic RL and ~630 training instances, point estimates alone are insufficient (e.g., 46.75% vs 44.88% vs Dr.GRPO unclear if meaningful)
Generalization concerns: all experiments on Qwen3 family only; unclear applicability to other model families, RL algorithms beyond GRPO, or domains beyond tool-use

Missing relevant comparisons: no baselines for simpler error-handling strategies (rejection sampling, prompt-based retry, rule-based handlers) or empirical comparison with other recent error-driven synthesis methods

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear evidence of error recovery gap between models (Figure 1)
Sound three-stage framework that converts sparse negative signals into dense on-policy corrective supervision
Comprehensive ablation studies (Table 2) isolating contributions of fission mechanism vs. Error Simulator
Detailed qualitative analysis with compelling case studies (Figure 6) showing learned diagnostic strategies
Reproducibility: detailed algorithms, prompts, and training pipeline provided in appendices
Consistent improvements across multiple model scales (1.7B, 4B, 8B)
Well-articulated decomposition of performance gains into one-shot success vs. error recovery rates
weaknesses: CRITICAL: Evaluation on single benchmark only (BFCL v4 Multi-Turn). Generalization to other error-recovery scenarios, domains, and benchmarks entirely unvalidated
Error Simulator quality never quantified: no accuracy measurements, failure mode analysis, or out-of-distribution robustness evaluation
Computational overhead unresolved: fission mechanism multiplies rollouts by G' per error, but no wall-clock time comparisons or practical cost/accuracy trade-offs provided
Modest improvements over strong baselines: 1.87% over Dr.GRPO (44.88→46.75%), with no statistical significance testing despite small margins
Design choices appear ad-hoc: time-dependent reward weights, δ_corr=1.0 threshold, and LIFO buffer all lack ablations or theoretical justification
One-shot success improvement minimal (+1.75% average), suggesting method narrowly targets error recovery rather than general tool-use capability
Distribution mismatch claim (key motivation) unvalidated: no empirical comparison between offline error-correction data and on-policy fission approach
Gradient collapse problem identified but not directly addressed: resampling adds examples but no analysis of actual variance reduction or gradient quality in Stage 3
Statistical rigor absent: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests for any results
Error Simulator training uses ground truth τ_gt in prompt (Figure 5), creating potential information leakage and limiting applicability to true online settings
Limited dataset scale (630 instances after filtering from 2K): no learning curves or justification of adequacy
Incomplete error analysis: no explanation for heterogeneous improvements across categories (Miss Param +1.2% vs. Long Context +11.8%)

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Identifies genuine limitation of smaller models failing to recover from errors in multi-turn tool use with clear demonstration of hallucinated retry loops
Clear and intuitive methodology: Three-stage framework is well-explained with effective visualizations; fission mechanism is conceptually well-motivated

Comprehensive experimental validation: Consistent improvements across model scales, appropriate baselines, thorough ablations (feedback quality, trigger frequency), and error recovery decomposition analysis
Learned Error Simulator: Clever approach to generate realistic feedback while avoiding target leakage through non-revealing descriptions
On-policy alignment via LIFO buffer: Keeps recent errors prioritized to maintain alignment with policy's current error distribution vs static offline datasets
Solid empirical results: 5.7% improvement in error recovery rate, 4% overall accuracy improvement on Qwen3-8B; outperforms specialized 8B tool agents
Reproducibility: Algorithm 1, hyperparameters, training details, and prompt templates provided in appendices
weaknesses: Limited evaluation scope: Restricted to BFCL v4 Multi-Turn benchmark only; missing evaluation on StableToolBench or evaluation in other tool-use domains (code, web navigation)
Insufficient Error Simulator analysis: Trained on only ~2K filtered instances; quality/robustness not validated, no sensitivity analysis to simulator accuracy, no evaluation of failure modes
Underspecified computational overhead: Resampling adds cost but total training time/compute not compared to baselines; overhead quantification remains open
Modest improvements for practical model sizes: 4% absolute gain for Qwen3-8B (practical target); improvements scale inversely with model size (160% for 1.7B, ~9% for 8B)

Incomplete theoretical justification: Lacks analysis of why fission works; unclear if benefit comes from training data quantity or conditioning on feedback; variance restoration claim (Eq. 6) not rigorously justified
Reward function design not ablated: Three weighted components with time-dependent schedules; no sensitivity analysis or ablation on which components are critical for error recovery

Training data scale concerns: Only 630 high-quality instances after filtering; unclear how much benefit comes from mechanism vs curated data quality; missing comparison of GRPO on same filtered dataset
Incomplete failure analysis: Limited discussion of cases where FISSION-GRPO still fails; no systematic characterization of challenging error types; case study is single-example
Distribution mismatch claim not quantified: Motivation around offline data mismatch is intuitive but never formally demonstrated; unclear how much this affects GRPO in practice
Baseline comparison caveat: External agent comparisons (ToolACE, BitAgent) use different base models; unclear if gains come from FISSION-GRPO mechanism or Qwen3 architecture

strengths: Well-motivated problem with compelling empirical evidence (Figure 1b); clear gap between small (Qwen3-8B ~20%) and large (Claude Sonnet ~50%) model error recovery rates
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three benchmarks (BFCL v4, TAU-Bench, TAU2-Bench), multiple model scales (1.7B, 4B, 8B), and strong baselines (GRPO, DAPO, Dr.GRPO, AWPO)

Thorough ablations isolating Error Simulator contribution (Table 2), compute-matched comparison (Table 4) validating efficiency gains, and cross-domain evaluation with human validation (96% non-leakage, Cohen's κ=0.71)
Consistent improvements across settings: 5.7% error recovery gain for Qwen3-8B, 4.0% overall accuracy (42.75%→46.75%), with gains up to +17.4% on TAU benchmarks
Thoughtful framework design with hybrid feedback synthesis, LIFO buffering, and principled data curation (630 high-quality instances from hierarchical filtering pipeline)
Strong reproducibility: detailed Algorithm 1, prompt templates, hyperparameter documentation, and promised code release
Effective qualitative analysis (Figure 7) illustrating progression from model collapse → hallucination → active diagnosis, providing interpretable insights beyond metrics
weaknesses: Critical concern about Error Simulator requiring ground-truth tool calls (τgt) at inference time; unclear how this constraint is satisfied in deployment, and claim of 'preventing target leakage' contradicts conditioning on τgt

Limited algorithmic novelty: core mechanism is straightforward resampling from augmented contexts with supervised feedback generation—incremental integration into GRPO rather than fundamental innovation

Error Simulator trained on only ~2K synthetic examples with single teacher (Claude Sonnet 4); no comparison with alternative error feedback methods; potential for teacher bias; robustness to out-of-distribution errors unclear

Critical design choices lack justification: LIFO buffering vs. alternatives (FIFO, random), reward component ablations (Eq. 2), trigger interval N setting, and correctness threshold δcorr=1 all set empirically without systematic analysis
No statistical significance testing: results lack error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple-seed validation; improvements of 4-5% in some categories may not be robust to initialization variance

Incomplete baseline comparisons: ToolACE and LoopTool cited as related but not directly compared; only RL baselines included; external agent results show unusual patterns (0.9% on TAU Retail) suggesting potential evaluation issues

Limited domain coverage in evaluation: three benchmarks share similar tool-calling structure; all training data synthetically generated; real API error distributions and deployment scenarios not tested
Uneven performance across error categories (Miss Param: 38% for 8B vs. Base: 57.5%), no failure mode analysis, and unclear when/why method underperforms suggest incomplete understanding
Scalability to larger models (13B+) unclear; unknown whether error recovery naturally improves with scale, making the method's general applicability uncertain

Insufficient ablations on reward design (time-dependent weighting, α=0.5), LIFO strategy justification, and sensitivity analysis of critical hyperparameters (N, δcorr) raise concerns about design choices

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear evidence of error recovery bottleneck in smaller models
Clear, well-structured methodology with intuitive three-stage framework effectively visualized
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across three benchmarks (BFCL v4, TAU-Bench, TAU2-Bench) and multiple model scales (1.7B-8B)
Thorough ablation studies including error recovery decomposition, feedback quality analysis, and cross-domain simulator generalization with human evaluation (96% non-leakage, κ=0.71)
Good reproducibility with detailed hyperparameters, pseudocode, prompt templates, and promised code release
Stable training dynamics without optimization collapse (Figure 5) and analysis of trigger frequency trade-offs
weaknesses: Limited novelty: method combines existing techniques (GRPO, error feedback, resampling) without fundamental algorithmic innovation; core contribution is engineering-focused application rather than novel framework

Narrow evaluation scope restricted to tool-use domain with interactive error feedback and retry mechanics; no evaluation on other iterative domains (code debugging, web navigation) or real-world APIs with realistic error distributions

Error Simulator critical concerns: trained on only ~2K instances with unclear provenance; unaddressed distribution mismatch between supervised training (ground-truth pairs) and actual policy errors during training; generalization validated on only 2 out-of-domain datasets
Modest empirical gains (4% overall accuracy improvement) do not clearly justify added complexity and computational overhead of generating G' additional rollouts per error

Missing key experimental comparisons: no baseline against simpler error feedback (rule-based/template), no comparison with offline error-correction datasets, no evaluation against recent self-correction methods, no analysis of when/why method works

Methodological concerns: threshold δ_corr=1.0 only catches complete failures; complex reward design (Eq. 2) lacks sensitivity analysis; LIFO buffering strategy not validated against alternatives; no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals
Evaluation metrics: 'error recovery rate' assumes unrealistic unlimited retry budget; artificial metric; overall improvements on more realistic metrics are modest
Error recovery rate specific to benchmarks with interactive feedback mechanisms; results may not generalize to real deployment scenarios with expensive APIs or different agent strategies

strengths: Well-motivated problem identification: Clear demonstration that smaller models fail to recover from execution errors and fall into hallucinated retry loops, with quantitative evidence (Figure 1b shows only ~20% recovery rate for Qwen3-8B vs. 50%+ for Claude Sonnet 4)

Sound and well-designed technical approach: Three-stage framework directly addresses limitations of standard RL (sparse negative rewards) and static datasets (distribution mismatch). The fission mechanism is intuitive and well-motivated

Comprehensive experimental validation: Consistent improvements across three independent benchmarks (BFCL v4, TAU-Bench, TAU2-Bench), three model scales (1.7B, 4B, 8B), and outperforms specialized agents (ToolACE-2-8B by +9.75%)

Thorough ablation studies: Error recovery decomposition (§4.3), feedback quality analysis (§4.4) isolating fission vs. simulator contributions, cross-domain error simulator evaluation (§4.5) with 96% non-leakage and κ=0.71, and compute-matched comparison (§4.6)
Strong reproducibility: Code availability promised, detailed Algorithm 1, explicit hyperparameters, prompt templates, training curves, and transparent data construction pipeline enable verification
Excellent presentation quality: Clear narrative flow, well-designed visualizations (particularly Figures 2, 3, 7), and intuitive explanations of problem and solution
Practical impact on smaller models: Demonstrates that careful training design can help smaller models approach larger model robustness, relevant for on-device and low-latency deployments
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: Core insight (explicitly teach error recovery during RL) is intuitive but not deeply novel. Fission mechanism is essentially conditional resampling—a straightforward extension of GRPO. Error Simulator is standard fine-tuned LLM with no novel modeling approach. Contribution feels incremental rather than fundamentally advancing understanding

Critical absence of statistical rigor: No error bars, confidence intervals, or significance testing despite inherent noise in RL environments. Results appear to be single runs; on some benchmarks improvements are modest (TAU2-Retail: 32.0 vs. 26.0) and statistical significance unclear. Expected standard for empirical SOTA claims

Generalization concerns: Training on only 630 instances from 11 curated domains; no ablation demonstrates this is optimal trade-off between quality/scale. Error Simulator relies on ~2K instances annotated by Claude Sonnet 4—potential for bias distillation. Cross-domain evaluation limited to 2 new domains with only 100 human-eval samples

Hyperparameter sensitivity underexplored: Critical threshold δ_corr=1.0 chosen 'empirically' without sensitivity analysis. Learning rate 1e-6 is exceptionally low without justification. Other parameters (buffer trigger, group size, deduplication) not analyzed. Figure 4 shows trigger frequency effects but over limited range without principled guidance for selection

Error Simulator evaluation gaps: No systematic failure case analysis—when does simulator produce misleading feedback? Simulator requires ground-truth calls as input (oracle assumption not clearly flagged). 96% non-leakage via human judgment is weaker than automated metrics. Teacher distillation from Claude may embed specific error-response biases

Insufficient failure mode analysis: Only one case study (§4.7) showing success. No systematic characterization of error categories where method underperforms (Figure 3 shows variability: Miss Param +7.4% vs. others much lower, but root causes unexplored). Missing: which error types remain problematic?

Limited scope of evaluation and baselines: Evaluation restricted to tool-calling agents with interactive retry feedback; unclear if insights transfer to code debugging, web navigation, or other error-recovery domains. All RL baselines recent (2025); missing comparison with classical approaches (Reflexion) and other error-recovery methods mentioned in related work (Paladin, CriticTool)

Reward design and on-policy alignment not fully justified: Normalization by 3 in Eq. 2 appears ad-hoc; time-dependent weight schedules lack principled justification; no ablation on reward strategy. LIFO buffering improves on-policy alignment but no KL measurement between correction batch and current policy reported

Incomplete analysis of practical considerations: Wall-clock training time and inference overhead not quantified beyond compute-matched updates. No analysis of how performance scales with training data size. Sensitivity to Error Simulator quality (using lower-quality base model) unexplored. Distribution of gains across single-turn vs. multi-turn trajectories not analyzed
